family: counter with a halving carry wave (Collatz-like)
summary: A counter whose digits are blocks of 1s: each cycle starts a carry wave that halves the digits it passes while they are odd; proved in Lean that it halts iff a wave reaches the left end carrying 2^t - 1 (halts_iff); no halt for 9·10<sup>52</sup> steps; open (Collatz-like).
title: What is known about 1RB1RC_1LC0LE_1RD1RC_1LB0RA_---0LF_1RD1LF
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RC_1LC0LE_1RD1RC_1LB0RA_---0LF_1RD1LF.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, but reduced to arithmetic. Lean proves (kernel) that the machine halts from blank tape exactly when an explicit map on lists of numbers reaches none: when a carry wave arrives at the left end of the tape with the value 1, i.e. when the value carried onto the leftmost digit is of the form 2t−1. Iterating the map exactly shows no halt for the first 9·1052 steps; heuristically the chance of a halt is negligible.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (E0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 42,663 cells have been visited and 42,644 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.53).

claims.title: Shift rules
claims.text: For every length n of the run and any tape around it: L C> 1^n R reaches L 1^n C> R; L 1^n F> 1 R reaches L F> 1 1^n R. These are the moves the head makes across the long uniform stretches of the tape.

claims.title: Halting is equivalent to an arithmetic iteration
claims.text: HaltsFromBlank ↔ ∃ k, iter k = none, where iter iterates the digit map next from the digits [26, 13, 9, 6] of the first cycle start (step 6,053). One cycle (5,009 steps) starts a wave on the last digit plus 61; on an odd value a the wave leaves a/2+1 behind and adds a/2 to the next digit; on an even value it stops (the digit becomes a/2+3, the next digit grows by a/2); at the left end of the tape the value 1 halts (E reads a 0 five steps later). Every piece is a symbolic trace checked by Lean; the composition is by induction.

claims.title: No halt in the first 9·10<sup>52</sup> steps
claims.text: The digit map iterated exactly (Python integers, with the step count of every piece), accelerated by memoizing the effect of the lowest digits until a wave leaves them: 29 visits of the left end, none with the value 1. The map and its step counts were compared with the direct run at every cycle start up to 5·10<sup>7</sup> steps, and the accelerated run with the plain map up to 2·10<sup>6</sup> cycles.

claims.title: Almost surely it never halts
claims.text: A halt needs the value carried onto the leftmost digit to be 2<sup>t</sup>−1, all ones in binary. These values grow by a few bits per visit of the left end (85 bits by 10<sup>52</sup> steps) and most of them are even; if their bits were random the chance of ever seeing all ones from here on would be below 2<sup>-80</sup>.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Open: equivalent (Lean) to whether the digit iteration ever delivers 2<sup>t</sup>−1 to the left end, a Collatz-like question about the binary digits of the carried values.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows, but the question is now arithmetic. This machine is a counter whose digits are blocks of 1s. Every so often a carry wave runs through the digits, halving each one it passes, and the machine stops only if that wave ever reaches the far end of the tape carrying exactly the number 1.

facts.text: Lean: halting is equivalent to an explicit iteration on lists of numbers.
No halt in the exact iteration of that map.
The only way to halt: the wave brings an all-ones binary number to the left end.

sections.heading: A counter whose digits are blocks of 1s
html: Stop the machine whenever the head is at the right end of the tape in state A, on a 1. The tape is then always a row of blocks of 1s, each followed by exactly one 0. Read the block lengths as the digits of a counter. The last four are always 14 7 6 4; the free digits sit to their left.

One cycle of 5,009 steps works only on the right end of the tape: it adds 48 to the last free digit and then starts a carry wave on it, a zigzag of the head that moves two cells of a digit per pass, one to each side, until the digit is used up. The wave sees the digit with 61 more cells than it had at the cycle start.

sections.heading: The carry wave halves the digits it passes
html:
On a digit holding a cells the wave does one of two things:

  • a odd: the digit is replaced by (a−1)/2 + 1, the other half, (a−1)/2, is added to the next digit to the left, and the wave moves on to that digit;
  • a even: the digit becomes a/2 + 3, the next digit to the left grows by a/2, and the wave stops. The head runs back to the right end, to the next cycle start.

So a carry travels left through odd values, as in a binary counter, and the digits get bigger towards the left. A real example from the run, starting at step 2,705,689 with the digits 26 756 730 292 232 114: the wave meets 127, 295, 439, 949 (all odd) and stops on 1230 (even), leaving 641 618 475 220 148 64, which is exactly what the machine has on its tape at step 4,073,393.

At the left end of the tape there is no next digit: the wave goes on into the blank part, halving the value again and again while it stays odd. The machine halts exactly when this reaches the value 1, and that happens exactly when the value arriving on the leftmost digit is 2t−1, a number whose binary digits are all ones.

Run the counter. These are the machine's own digits at its first cycle start (left to right, the last four are the fixed ones). Each click is one cycle: the wave starts on the last free digit plus 61 and moves left. The digits it changed are marked.

sections.heading: What Lean checks
html:
The rule above is not just observed: Lean proves, for every value of the digits, that the machine does exactly this. A Python script runs the machine symbolically on tapes with unknown block lengths and writes a Lean proof of each piece: the cycle, the start of the wave on a digit, one zigzag, the two ways a zigzag ends, the run back across one digit, the end of the run, and the halt. A hand-written file then glues the pieces: any number of zigzags (induction), the run back over any list of digits (induction on the list), the wave over any number of digits (induction again), and the left end (strong induction on the value).

The main theorem, halts_iff, says: the machine halts from blank tape if and only if iterating the digit map from [26, 13, 9, 6] ever gives none. The Lean kernel checked it; it uses no unproved assumptions.

sections.heading: A question about binary digits
html:
Whether the map ever gives none is a question about numbers only. Iterated exactly, it shows no halt for the first 9·1052 steps of the machine. Waves reach the leftmost digit rarely (once every several times more cycles than the previous time), and the values they bring grow: 7, 11, 10, 13, 17, 19, 23, 29 bits in the first 2·107 cycles, 85 bits by 1052 steps. A halt needs one of them to be all ones in binary. If the bits behaved like coin flips the chance would shrink like 2−bits at every visit, and it is already far below one in a trillion trillion.

So the machine almost surely runs forever, but proving it means showing that this deterministic process never produces 2t−1. That is a Collatz-like problem: easy to state, with no known method to settle it.

sections.heading: The same machine under another name
html: 1RB1RA_1LC0RC_1RE0LD_0RE0LF_1RA---_1RB1LF is another holdout of the same group. Its table is different, but at every cycle start it has exactly the same tape (in state C instead of A, and a few hundred steps later). The difference is in how the head travels: there, the run back to the right end shifts a double 0 through the digits; here, state C simply walks over them. Both machines have their own Lean proof of the same reduction.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.53).
After 109 steps the tape spans 42,663 cells (17 left of the start, 30,165 right), with a density of 1s of 1.0.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.
